topic: Mantis shrimp: punch force, cavitation, color vision, club armor
hook: A shrimp that punches 2,500x its body weight

slides.title: Faster than a blink
slides.body: Its club-like arm strikes at up to 23 meters per second, finishing in just a few milliseconds.
slides.image_prompt: Colorful mantis shrimp on a coral reef, club arm poised to strike, dramatic underwater lighting

slides.title: Two hits in one
slides.body: The strike is so fast it creates collapsing bubbles in the water, hitting the prey a second time.
slides.image_prompt: Burst of tiny bubbles collapsing underwater next to a cracked snail shell, high-speed photo style

slides.title: 12 color receptors
slides.body: Humans see color with 3 types of cones. Mantis shrimp have 12 types of color receptors.
slides.image_prompt: Extreme close-up of mantis shrimp striped compound eyes on stalks, vivid rainbow colors

slides.title: But worse at color
slides.body: Tests show they tell similar colors apart worse than we do. They likely recognize colors fast, not finely.
slides.image_prompt: Mantis shrimp facing two nearly identical colored light panels underwater, soft glow

slides.title: Armor engineers copy
slides.body: Its club has a spiral fiber structure that stops cracks. Scientists study it to design tougher materials.
slides.image_prompt: Spiral layered fiber structure like a twisted staircase, glowing blue, cross-section of a tough material

cta: Follow for a new wild fact every day
caption:
A mantis shrimp's punch can hit with forces over 2,500 times its own body weight, and it's fast enough to make the water itself strike its prey a second time.

The twist: with 12 color receptors to our 3, you'd expect super color vision. Experiments found they're actually worse than us at telling close colors apart. (Sources: Patek et al., Nature 2004; Thoen et al., Science 2014)
